Serbian student coalition brings down strongman Vučić in electoral upset. But no PM in sight

The student-led victory in Serbia is expected to reverberate across Europe, adding momentum to youth and student protests that have shaken governments across the continent.

Debdutta Chakraborty

26 October, 2026 07:02 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Supporters of the electoral list 'Student List - Students Win' celebrate after Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia | REUTERS/Uros Arsic

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: In an unprecedented electoral upset in the Balkans, a student-led coalition brought down the far-right’s decade-old hold on Serbia. But no one knows who the next Prime Minister will be. Far right leader Aleksandar Vučić lost to a student-led movement in snap elections Sunday in what is being called a new political era in Belgrade.

The electoral outcome followed an extraordinary period of protests against corruption and government negligence, culminating in a pivotal moment that resulted in a voter turnout reported to be the highest in 30 years.

Vučić, who was PM for three years from 2014 to 2017 and President for nine years since then, conceded defeat after more than a decade of political dominance as the student-led movement won a decisive majority in the country’s 250-seat parliament.

Show Full Article

The election became, in effect, a referendum on Serbia’s political future: whether the country would continue under Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party, known as the SNS, or a movement promising to restore democratic institutions, strengthen the rule of law and confront corruption. The youth-backed Students’ List, will take between 135 and 140 seats. The SNS got 105 seats.

Following Vučić’s resignation in September, Serbian Parliament Speaker Ana Brnabić assumed presidential duties. Vučić claimed he stepped down to contest the 25 October parliamentary election in a bid to become prime minister. Serbia must now hold presidential elections in the coming months to elect a successor and determine who will serve as the country’s next head of state.

The student movement, meanwhile, began in 2024 with students blockading streets after a concrete canopy collapsed outside the railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, killing 16 people.

Within less than two years, it grew into a nationwide campaign that brought together people from across Serbian society, including farmers, actors, judges, academics and other citizens disillusioned with the government.

The students had no obvious leaders and little conventional political experience. Yet their ‘Student List—Students Win’ movement attracted anti-government voters across the country. They fielded candidates for all 250 parliamentary seats, but no students appeared on the list. For now, they have not announced their PM candidate.

Serbia’s former President and Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia | REUTERS/Zorana Jevtic The victory marked a reversal for Vučić, an ultranationalist who cultivated an image as a pragmatic leader balancing ties with the European Union, Russia, China, and Israel. Born in Belgrade in 1970, Vučić entered politics in 1993 with Vojislav Šešelj’s far right Serbian Radical Party (SRS) and drew condemnation for his infamous 1995 parliamentary outburst to kill 100 Muslims for every Serb killed, nine days after the Srebrenica genocide.

In 2008, he left SRS over the party’s support for Serbia’s EU membership and co-founded SNS, a centre to far right party which later emerged as Serbia’s largest party in 2012. Vučić went on to consolidate a dominant-party system while pursuing EU accession, economic liberalisation and dialogue with Kosovo. The SNS ruled Serbia from 2012 to 2026.

Also Read: Brazil nips Latin America’s Trump tide with dramatic win for Lula: ‘Nobody’s backyard’

Will Serbia now be part of EU? The student movement’s programme offers little clarity on its international priorities, while its statements suggest it could maintain the outgoing government’s positions on two contentious issues.

In a May 2026 memorandum, the movement described Kosovo as an “inalienable and integral part of Serbia” and a component of Serbian national identity, advocating a settlement within Serbia’s constitutional framework. In September, it opposed sanctions on Russia, which the outgoing government has also refused to support. Whether these positions would carry over into government remains unclear.

Public opinion among supporters of the student-backed list also suggests an appetite for closer European ties: 75 percent favour stronger relations with the EU, compared with just 10 percent who prefer closer relations with Russia.

Serbia applied for European Union membership in December 2009, received candidate status in March 2012 and formally began accession negotiations in January 2014. Accession progress has remained slow amid EU concerns over the rule of law, press freedom, Serbia’s limited alignment with the bloc’s foreign policy and sanctions against Russia, and the unresolved status of Kosovo.

The Kosovo-Serbia conflict is a political and territorial dispute rooted in ethnic tensions between Albanians and Serbs. The conflict escalated into the 1998–1999 Kosovo War and remains unresolved, with Serbia continuing to refuse recognition of Kosovo’s independence.

EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa however welcomed the outcome, voicing hope for a reset in relations with Serbia, despite the student movement’s unclear position on European integration.

The election was also watched internationally as part of 10 pivotal days of voting around the world, in which right-wing forces face off against pro-democracy movements. The student-led victory in Serbia is expected to reverberate across Europe, adding momentum to youth and student protests that have shaken governments across the continent.

I have just spoken by phone with the leaders of the Students' List @studentblokade , who won the elections in Serbia, to congratulate them on their victory. I assured them of Hungary’s support. I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during…

— Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) October 25, 2026

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar was the first EU national leader to congratulate the victors, comparing their success with his own win over Viktor Orbán earlier this year. “I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle,” he added on X.

A tragedy that became a national movement In Serbia, what began as weekly student demonstrations after the 2024 tragedy grew into a movement demanding justice on university campuses and city streets and soon spread into communities. Farmers, actors, judges and other groups joined the protests, turning a student campaign into a broader challenge to the government.

In January 2025, Prime Minister Miloš Vučević resigned, saying the move was intended to “defuse tensions”. Two months later, Belgrade witnessed what was described as Serbia’s largest-ever anti-government protest.

As the movement grew, students organised themselves through assemblies, or plenums, rather than relying on a conventional leadership structure. The decentralised approach allowed the campaign to expand while maintaining its identity as a movement driven by students and ordinary citizens rather than established political figures.

By the time Vučić announced snap elections in September, the protesters had begun converting their public momentum into an organised electoral campaign. They staged rallies, visited rural areas that had long been Vučić strongholds and went door-to-door, presenting themselves as anti-establishment candidates. Their slogan was blunt: “Serbia or Mafia?”

Initially, Vučić sought to describe the protesters as “well-intentioned.” Ahead of the election, however, he accused them of trying to “bring down” Serbia. Even after conceding defeat Sunday night, the 56-year-old alleged that the movement had the backing of unnamed “European countries and the American deep state”.

Also Read: France to Italy, cost-of-living protests rock EU: Stores looted, 140-year-old landmark set on fire

What is Student List’s programme? The elected members of parliament will be responsible for delivering what amounts to the movement’s manifesto. The students have said they were looking for people who could enter public institutions and “do their jobs responsibly and not forget why they are there”.

Under an 11-point programme, the student movement wants to eradicate corruption by establishing a police unit to arrest those responsible for it, purge the internal affairs ministry of officials who broke rules while cracking down on protesters or who have links to organised crime, reform Serbia’s media landscape and free the public broadcaster from political control, and end political patronage in public enterprises by stopping the recruitment of party loyalists.

Although the students themselves have not been elected, they are the ones who made promises to the Serbian people. They will, therefore, face pressure to ensure that the parliamentary representatives they selected follow through on the movement’s manifesto.

For his part, Vučić has shown little sign of accepting the movement’s victory as the end of his political struggle. In the speech to party supporters on Sunday evening, he said the students had destroyed two years of life in Serbia and would be defeated “faster by a campaign demanding accountability for a tragedy to a national political force challenging the government itself”.

Who will run Serbia now? The students’ victory has created a new political challenge: identifying who will govern the country. According to reports, it will not be the students themselves, because they did not stand for election. The movement appears to have judged that voters might be reluctant to support a parliamentary list made up of candidates with little life experience.

Although Ilija Srdanović, a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, topped the Student List, he is not widely regarded as the most likely candidate for prime minister. At least 135 people on the list are thought to have won seats in parliament. They include former basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, who was 24th on the list; renowned actor Tihomir Stanić, who was eighth; opera singer Nikola Mikić, who was 46th; and Dejan Šoškić, the former governor of the National Bank of Serbia, who was 27th. The list also includes a substantial number of professors.

Šoškić’s name has been mentioned in connection with the top government post. He has spoken about economic reforms he would pursue and has faced extensive criticism in pro-government media.

The absence of a clearly established leadership could also complicate the transition from protest to government. A movement that drew strength from its decentralised structure will now have to make decisions, negotiate political differences and manage institutions.

The Russia pivot Vučić’s political defeat also carries implications for Serbia’s foreign relationships. He campaigned aggressively through round-the-clock coverage on pro-government media, attacking his opponents as ‘foreign mercenaries’. He contrasted their campaign with his own plans to build prosperity through new roads and hospitals.

In the process, he moved away from the pro-EU positioning that had helped his populist party come to power in 2012, repeatedly boasting of the support of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Speaking to the state broadcaster RTS during the campaign, Vučić claimed Putin understood that there would be no sanctions against Russia only if the populists won. “It is no coincidence that Vladimir Putin said he hopes that I will be the prime minister.”

His relationship with Moscow has been a prominent feature of his political positioning. In September, Vučić defied the EU by allowing what it describes as a hero’s funeral in Belgrade for Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb army commander convicted of genocide by a UN court.

Vučić has also enjoyed strong support from China’s President Xi Jinping. The two leaders have described their relationship as an “ironclad friendship.”

Xi has consistently backed Vučić politically, sending high-profile congratulations following his re-election victories and expressing support for Serbia’s national sovereignty. In May, during Vučić’s state visit to Beijing, Xi personally awarded him China’s Friendship Medal, the country’s highest state honour for foreign nationals.

(Edited by Tony Rai)

Dutch govt plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul

The govt wants to save €900 mn a year by 2027, rising to €3.5 billion from 2035. The cabinet will also present plans for deploying AI to work more productively early next year.

Patrick Van Oosterom

26 October, 2026 05:56 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

The Dutch Parliament building beside the Hofvijver pond in The Hague, Netherlands, on Thursday, March 18, 2021. Caretaker prime minister Mark Ruttes center-right party, the VVD, won 36 seats in the 150-strong parliament, with the pro-European group D66 in second place with 24 seats, according to a projection early Thursday by Dutch news agency ANP with 63% of votes counted.

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

The Dutch government aims to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive targeting annual savings of €3.5 billion ($3.9 billion).

The central government wants to save €900 million a year by 2027, rising to €3.5 billion from 2035. That amounts to around 25,000 jobs, spread over several years, according to a government statement on Monday. The cabinet will present plans for deploying artificial intelligence to work more productively early next year.

“We cannot keep doing what we have been doing,” State Secretary for Effective Government Eric van den Burg said. “That is why we are going to make tough choices for a central government that really works: simpler, smarter, and smaller.”

Show Full Article

The number of government officials surged to a record 160,000 at the end of 2025, up 41% compared to 2018, despite pledges by previous cabinets to scale back headcount.

The Dutch government budget deficit of 1.8% is one of the smallest in the European Union. Yet the figure and its long-term outlook still raise concerns in the Netherlands, which has a reputation for being fiscally conservative.

Officials from Mecca pact countries to meet Iranian officials in Tehran

Reuters

26 October, 2026 02:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Andrew Mills and Ariba Shahid Oct 26 (Reuters) – Top officials from Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are to meet Iran’s leaders in Tehran on Monday in their first high-level contact since the kingdom became a pressure point in the wider Iran conflict.

Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said.

Attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have spiralled in recent weeks and rhetoric between Washington and Tehran has grown more heated. Both countries have also drawn up plans to restart the wider war, possibly after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Show Full Article

Monday’s planned talks will be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into the conflict. Under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday discussions on regional security would include “Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran.”

Baghaei said the meeting, proposed during a visit by Munir to Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms based on the interests of countries in the region.

Qatari mediators met Iranian officials in Tehran on Sunday in a push to de-escalate regional tensions, Reuters reported. Qatar has, for months, played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington.

A senior Iranian official said the meeting was initiated by Pakistan, during Munir’s visit to Tehran, as he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.

Earlier mediation efforts involving both Pakistan and Qatar helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later.

The deputy secretary of Iran’s top security body, Ali Baqeri-Kani, told state TV that Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid, Pakistan’s Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin would visit Tehran for consultations with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on regional security.

Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the meeting is part of ongoing efforts by the Mecca Pact countries to de-escalate the current crisis, promote diplomatic solutions, and support mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan.     “The visit also underscores the pivotal role of the Mecca Pact states in fostering regional security and stability, and their commitment to working with all nations in the region toward achieving this goal,” Krimly posted on X.

Pakistan’s military media wing and Turkey’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

TENSIONS RISING

Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued unabated.

Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.

Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran and Iran’s leaders have said that a renewed US military campaign would be met with a stronger response than before.

Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again. A US intelligence memo this week warned that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached “advanced stages”.

The war, now nearly eight months old, has weighed on President Donald Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the midterms.

The Mecca agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.

Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

(Reporting by Andrew Mills and Ariba Shahid; Additional reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu and Parisa Hafezi; Writing by Andrew Mills, Yomna Ehab and Eman Abouhassira; Editing by Christopher Cushing, Tom Hogue and Saad Sayeed)

Russia says it caught Ukrainian agents preparing close range drone attack on Moscow’s air defences

Reuters

26 October, 2026 02:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

MOSCOW, Oct 26 (Reuters) – Russia’s FSB security service has thwarted a planned Ukrainian drone attack from inside Russia on a key element of Moscow’s air defence system and on an electricity facility, the FSB said on Monday, saying it had arrested two men involved in the plot.

The two men, who the FSB said were from the South Caucasus region and had been acting under instructions from Ukraine’s SBU security service, had retrieved First Person View drones and explosives from two Russian regions, delivered them to the Moscow region, and configured and activated the drones, the FSB said. The drones were to be remotely controlled from Ukraine, it said.

“It has been established that one of the suspects was recruited by an SBU officer and, on that officer’s instructions and in return for a promised monetary reward, travelled to Russia to prepare and carry out a sabotage and terrorist attack. To this end, he enlisted the help of an acquaintance from his close circle,” the FSB said.

Show Full Article

“The suspects were detained by FSB officers while preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electricity infrastructure facility and on one of the key components of Moscow’s missile defence system,” it said.

There was no immediate comment from the SBU or from Ukraine, which has intensified its attempted drone attacks on the Russian capital in recent months, as Russia has stepped up its own attacks on Ukrainian power and other infrastructure targets.

(Reporting by Reuters; Writing by Anastasia Teterevleva; Editing by Andrew Osborn)
